title: Behind the Runny Nose
subtitle: Many years of a blocked nose, from the first visit to the operating room
description: Reading the first endoscopy, classifying the rhinitis, choosing the right IgE test, interpreting the result, choosing the first prescription under the 2024-2025 ARIA guidelines, managing a patient who came back on a decongestant, and what to do when correct treatment is not enough.

steps.title: Step 1/7: What the Scope Shows
steps.scenario: A 41-year-old man comes to clinic for the first time with a blocked, runny nose. You pass the endoscope.
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy at the first visit, unannotated: pale, boggy inferior turbinates with clear watery secretion. Caption: 'First visit.'
steps.question: What does the endoscopy show, and what is it most consistent with?

options.text: (A) Pale, swollen inferior turbinates with clear watery secretion, consistent with allergic rhinitis
(B) Dark red, congested turbinates, consistent with rebound from a decongestant spray
(C) Purulent secretion draining from the middle meatus, consistent with bacterial rhinosinusitis
(D) Polypoid mucosa filling the middle meatus, consistent with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The allergic nose has a look. The inferior turbinates are swollen but pale, sometimes almost bluish, and the mucosa is wet with thin clear secretion. The swelling is edema from the allergic reaction, not congestion from blood. Seeing this on the first visit tells you what you are treating before any test comes back, and it gives you a baseline to compare against later.

Why the others fail:
(B) Rebound congestion from a topical decongestant looks the opposite: the turbinates are beefy and dark red, and the mucosa looks dry and angry rather than wet. Keep this picture in mind; it comes up later.
(C) Pus in the middle meatus is infection, and it points to the sinuses rather than the turbinates. Thin clear secretion is not pus.
(D) Polyps are smooth, gray, glistening and insensate, and they sit in the middle meatus. Pale turbinates are not polyps.

Keypoint: pale, wet and swollen is allergy; red, dry and swollen is rebound; pus or polyps mean the sinuses.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) 2008 update. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. doi:10.1111/j.1398-9995.2007.01620.x.

steps.title: Step 2/7: How Bad, How Often
steps.scenario: You take the history. He has had bilateral nasal obstruction, watery rhinorrhea and postnasal drip for many years. The symptoms are there most days of the week, all year round. They wreck his concentration at work and wake him at night.
steps.media: Load image: Your own 2 x 2 table of the ARIA classification, redrawn, not reproduced. Rows: Intermittent (4 days a week or fewer, or 4 consecutive weeks or fewer) and Persistent (more than 4 days a week and more than 4 consecutive weeks). Columns: Mild (none of the following) and Moderate to severe (one or more of: sleep disturbance, impaired daily activities or leisure or sport, impaired work or school, troublesome symptoms). No cell highlighted. Caption: 'ARIA classification.'
steps.question: Using the classification shown, how do you classify his rhinitis?

options.text: (A) Intermittent, mild
(B) Intermittent, moderate to severe
(C) Persistent, moderate to severe
(D) Persistent, mild

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

ARIA classifies rhinitis on two axes. Duration: persistent means symptoms on more than 4 days a week and for more than 4 consecutive weeks; anything less is intermittent. Severity: moderate to severe means the symptoms disturb sleep, daily activities, work or school, or are simply troublesome; if none of those apply, it is mild. He has both: symptoms most days for years, and they cost him sleep and concentration.

The classification sets the starting point for treatment. Mild intermittent disease can start with an antihistamine alone. Moderate to severe disease, especially persistent, starts higher.

Before you prescribe, one more minute of history. The guideline is called Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma for a reason: the upper and lower airway share the same inflammation, and many patients with allergic rhinitis have asthma that nobody has named. Ask about wheeze, cough and chest tightness, and ask about itchy, watery eyes. The answers change what you prescribe and who else he needs to see.

Why the others fail:
(A) Fails on both axes. Most days for years is not intermittent, and lost sleep is not mild.
(B) Right on severity, wrong on duration. Intermittent means 4 days a week or fewer, or 4 weeks or fewer at a time.
(D) Right on duration, wrong on severity. Symptoms that wake him and affect his work are moderate to severe by definition.

Keypoint: how many days a week, how many weeks in a row, does it affect sleep or work, and is there a chest or an eye story too.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) 2008 update. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. doi:10.1111/j.1398-9995.2007.01620.x. Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.

steps.title: Step 3/7: Which Test
steps.scenario: You want to know whether this is allergic and, if so, to what. He mentions that his nose was itchy yesterday, so he took an antihistamine tablet.
steps.question: Which test do you order today?

options.text: (A) Total serum IgE
(B) Skin prick test today; one tablet does not affect it
(C) Skin prick test today with higher-concentration extracts to overcome the antihistamine
(D) Allergen-specific serum IgE today, or a skin prick test at a later visit once the antihistamine has cleared

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The question you are asking is: is this allergic, and to what? Two tests answer it, and they answer it the same way: a skin prick test or allergen-specific serum IgE, each run against the allergens he is likely exposed to. Both report sensitization to individual allergens. The skin test is cheaper and gives a result in 15 minutes; serum IgE is not affected by medication or skin condition. Today the antihistamine decides: it suppresses the wheal and flare the skin test depends on, and if the histamine positive control does not react, nothing on the panel can be read. So either send blood now or bring him back once the drug has cleared, usually a few days for a second-generation antihistamine.

Why the others fail:
(A) This is the mix-up to avoid. Total IgE does not tell you whether he is allergic or to what. It is raised in many conditions and normal in many allergic patients. It has a role in a different disease, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, where it is used as one marker of type 2 inflammation when deciding on a biologic. In allergic rhinitis it should not be ordered in place of allergen-specific IgE.
(B) One tablet is enough to blunt the skin response. Second-generation antihistamines act for about a day, and some persist longer.
(C) The extract is not the problem; the skin's ability to respond is. A stronger extract on suppressed skin gives an unreadable result and a higher chance of an irritant reaction.

Keypoint: in allergic rhinitis, order IgE against specific allergens, never total IgE; and if he took an antihistamine, use blood or come back.

Reference: Seidman MD, Gurgel RK, Lin SY, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Allergic Rhinitis. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;152(1 Suppl):S1-S43. Bousquet J, Anto JM, Bachert C, et al. Allergic rhinitis. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2020;6(1):95. doi:10.1038/s41572-020-00227-0. Bernstein JA, Bernstein JS, Makol R, Ward S. Allergic rhinitis: a review. JAMA. 2024;331(10):866-877.

steps.title: Step 4/7: Reading the Result
steps.scenario:
Serum specific IgE comes back:

    House dust mite (D. pteronyssinus)   class 4
    Cat dander                            class 2
    Grass pollen                          negative
    Total IgE                             60 kU/L

He has never owned a cat and does not react around them. He sleeps in a carpeted bedroom with a fabric headboard and his symptoms are the same all year.
steps.question: What does this result change?

options.text: (A) It confirms mite allergy, and he should also avoid cats, since he is sensitized to both
(B) It confirms allergic rhinitis to house dust mite, guides avoidance advice and immunotherapy candidacy, and does not change which spray to start
(C) A total IgE of 60 is below 100, so this is not type 2 disease and may not be allergic at all
(D) A class 4 mite result means severe disease and warrants going straight to immunotherapy

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

A positive specific IgE proves sensitization to that allergen. It does not by itself prove that allergen is causing his symptoms. The diagnosis of allergic rhinitis is the match between three things: the history, the endoscopic picture from Step 1, and a positive test to an allergen he is actually exposed to. House dust mite fits all three: year-round symptoms, a carpeted bedroom, class 4. Cat fits only one: he is sensitized, but he has no exposure and no symptoms around cats, so that result is not clinically relevant and does not need action.

What the result changes. It confirms the rhinitis is allergic rather than something else. It tells you which avoidance advice is worth his effort: mite covers, washing bedding hot, removing the carpet if he can, and nothing about cats. And it makes him a candidate for allergen immunotherapy later if medication does not control him, because immunotherapy needs a confirmed relevant allergen to target.

What it does not change. The first prescription. The 2024-2025 ARIA recommendations for intranasal and oral treatment do not depend on which allergen is found or how high the specific IgE is. Treatment is driven by severity and duration, which you settled in Step 2.

Why the others fail:
(A) Sensitization without exposure or symptoms is common and does not need avoidance. Telling him to avoid cats he never meets is advice with no benefit.
(C) The 100 kU/L cutoff belongs to a different disease. In chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, total IgE is one of several markers of type 2 tissue inflammation used when deciding whether a refractory patient qualifies for a biologic, and even there it is a weak discriminator: blood eosinophil count does most of the work, and total IgE is decisive in only a few percent of cases. In allergic rhinitis, total IgE plays no part in the diagnosis, and a normal value does not make him non-allergic. His specific IgE and his history already answered the question.
(D) Specific IgE class reports how much IgE is present, not how bad his symptoms are. Severity is the ARIA classification from Step 2. Immunotherapy is considered when pharmacotherapy fails, not as a first step because a number is high.

Keypoint: specific IgE proves sensitization, the history proves relevance, the two together make the diagnosis; the result guides avoidance and immunotherapy, and the spray is chosen by severity.

Reference: Seidman MD, Gurgel RK, Lin SY, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Allergic Rhinitis. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;152(1 Suppl):S1-S43. Bousquet J, Anto JM, Bachert C, et al. Allergic rhinitis. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2020;6(1):95. doi:10.1038/s41572-020-00227-0. Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131. Cho A, Cho HJ, Kim CH, Kwak K, Rha MS. Predictive value of blood eosinophil count and serum total IgE for type 2 chronic rhinosinusitis according to allergic sensitization status. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2026.

steps.title: Step 5/7: The First Prescription
steps.scenario: Persistent, moderate to severe allergic rhinitis, house dust mite confirmed. No asthma symptoms. He is on no medication and has never used a nasal spray properly.
steps.question: What do you prescribe first?

options.text: (A) A second-generation oral antihistamine alone
(B) Omalizumab, since IgE-mediated disease is now confirmed
(C) Montelukast plus an oral antihistamine
(D) A fixed-combination intranasal antihistamine and corticosteroid spray, such as azelastine-fluticasone

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The 2024-2025 ARIA revision changed this answer. For patients whose symptoms are unlikely to be controlled by a single agent, it gives a strong recommendation for the fixed INAH+INCS combination over no treatment, and a conditional recommendation for INAH+INCS over INCS alone, with the combination particularly favored in patients with more severe symptoms. Within the class it suggests azelastine-fluticasone over olopatadine-mometasone. The combination works faster than INCS alone, and patients report higher satisfaction and less need for extra medication.

An INCS alone remains reasonable where cost or availability is a problem; the guideline says so.

Why the others fail:
(A) Oral antihistamines work, and the guideline recommends them over nothing. But it also gives a strong recommendation for INCS over oral antihistamines, because INCS control nasal symptoms and quality of life better. For moderate to severe persistent disease, an oral antihistamine alone is under-treatment.
(B) This is the IgE mix-up applied to treatment. Anti-IgE therapy is approved as add-on treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps that is uncontrolled on intranasal steroids, and for asthma. It is not a treatment for allergic rhinitis, and confirming that his rhinitis is IgE-mediated does not make him a candidate. He has not yet tried a nasal spray.
(C) Montelukast carries important safety concerns, and the guideline gives a strong recommendation for oral antihistamines over leukotriene antagonists, plus a conditional recommendation against adding one to the other.

Keypoint: for moderate to severe disease, start with the INAH+INCS combination; if that is not available, INCS alone; a positive IgE is a diagnosis, not a reason for a biologic.

Reference: Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131. Vieira RJ, Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part II, Oral and Ocular Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:1947-1970. doi:10.1111/all.70305. Chhiba KD, Patel GB, Peters AT. Anti-IgE therapy in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2025.

steps.title: Step 6/7: Two Weeks Later
steps.scenario:
He is back after two weeks, as blocked as ever. He used the combination spray for three days, felt nothing, and stopped. He went back to a pharmacy spray he had used years ago that opens his nose within minutes, and has been using it three or four times a day for ten days. He now needs it more often to get the same effect.

On endoscopy the inferior turbinates are dark red and congested, and the mucosa looks dry.
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy at the second visit, unannotated: beefy, dark red, congested inferior turbinates. Caption: 'Two weeks later.'
steps.question: What do you do?

options.text: (A) Let him continue the decongestant for another two weeks as a bridge while the combination spray takes effect
(B) Add a short course of oral corticosteroid to break the congestion
(C) Stop the decongestant now, restart the combination spray with instruction on technique and on how long it takes to work, and review in four weeks
(D) Switch to an oral second-generation antihistamine, since he does not tolerate sprays

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Compare this scope with the first visit. Then the turbinates were pale, wet and swollen. Now they are dark red, dry and swollen. That is rebound congestion from a topical decongestant: the vessels stop responding and dilate harder as each dose wears off, so the nose ends up more blocked than before and the patient uses the spray more and more. The 2024-2025 ARIA revision now suggests against using these sprays for more than 5 days, and preferably less.

The fix is to stop the decongestant and restart the treatment he abandoned, with two things he was not told the first time. The combination spray takes days, not minutes, to work, so three days was not a fair trial. And technique matters: head neutral, nozzle angled away from the septum, gentle sniff. The guideline is explicit that its recommendations assume correct use. Warn him that the first week off the decongestant will feel worse before it feels better.

Why the others fail:
(A) The guideline suggests against combining an INCS with a decongestant: no added efficacy, more adverse events. Bridging is tolerated for under 5 days; he is already at ten. Two more weeks deepens the rebound.
(B) Oral steroids may shrink the mucosa briefly, but the congestion returns when the course ends, and he would still be on the decongestant. It treats the wrong problem.
(D) He does not have a spray intolerance; he has a spray he never gave a chance. Oral antihistamines are recommended over nothing, but INCS are recommended over oral antihistamines, and for moderate to severe disease an oral antihistamine alone is under-treatment.

Keypoint: dark red and dry is rebound; stop the decongestant, restart the right spray, and set expectations this time.

Reference: Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. ARIA-EAACI Guidelines 2024-2025 Revision: Part I, Intranasal Treatments. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.

steps.title: Step 7/7: Three Months Later
steps.scenario:
He returns after three months. Rhinorrhea and itch are much better. But he says the blockage is no better at all. You watch him use the spray: head neutral, nozzle angled away from the septum, gentle sniff. Technique is correct.

You perform nasal endoscopy. The septum is deviated posteriorly to the right, and both inferior turbinates are enlarged with no mucosal response to decongestant.
steps.media: Load image: Nasal endoscopy, unannotated, showing the posterior septal deviation to the right and the enlarged inferior turbinates. Caption: 'Three months later.'
steps.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Septoplasty with inferior turbinate reduction, and continue the intranasal treatment afterward
(B) Double the dose of the combination spray and review in another three months
(C) A short course of oral corticosteroid to break the cycle
(D) Surgery, after which the allergy treatment can stop

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The medication has done what medication can do: the itch and the running have settled. What is left is a fixed obstruction that no spray will change. A deviated septum is bone and cartilage. Inferior turbinates that do not shrink with a decongestant have submucosal hypertrophy rather than reversible swelling. Both are surgical problems. Septoplasty and turbinate reduction relieve the obstruction and, by opening the nose, also let the spray reach the mucosa it is meant to treat.

The operation does not remove the allergy. He still has house dust mite sensitization and he will still have inflammation. The spray continues after surgery.

One thing to check before any of this: technique. The ARIA guidelines assume correct use of intranasal sprays, and poor technique is a common reason for apparent failure. Here you watched him and it was fine, which is why the next step is endoscopy rather than another round of coaching.

Why the others fail:
(B) More of the same drug will not move a deviated septum. Three more months is three months of a blocked nose for nothing.
(C) Oral steroids may briefly shrink mucosa, but they do nothing for the septum, the turbinates return as soon as the course ends, and repeated courses carry real harm.
(D) Surgery corrects the anatomy, not the immunology. Stopping the spray afterward brings back the rhinorrhea and itch that it had controlled.

Keypoint: when the itch and the running are controlled but the blockage is not, look inside; medication does not treat anatomy.

Reference: Bousquet J, Khaltaev N, Cruz AA, et al. Allergy. 2008;63(Suppl 86):8-160. Sousa-Pinto B, Bousquet J, Vieira RJ, et al. Allergy. 2026;81:954-976. doi:10.1111/all.70131.
